newsitem.title: USA: Cuba hands U.S. a cocaine haul from Colombian ship.
newsitem.headline: Cuba hands U.S. a cocaine haul from Colombian ship.

text.p: In a rare show of cooperation, the Cuban government has handed over to U.S. authorities more than six tonnes of cocaine seized on a Colombian freighter, the U.S. Attorney's Office said on Thursday.

Cuban coast guard officers may come to Miami to testify in the trial of the captain and crew of the vessel, which sank off Cuba's coast in October, U.S. Attorney's Office spokesman Wilfredo Fernandez said.

Hostility between Cuba and the United States goes back more than 30 years and the two have no diplomatic relations. President Fidel Castro's government also stands accused by U.S. politicians of being in league with Colombian drug lords.

The freighter Limerick was sailing from Barranquilla, Colombia, to Freeport in the Bahamas in October when it began to founder in international waters about 12 miles (19 km) from the U.S. military base at Guantanamo in southeast Cuba.

The U.S. Coast Guard, which patrols the Caribbean to intercept drug smugglers, received permission to board from the captain and began to search the ship. When it began to take on more water it was abandoned and the captain and crew, mostly Colombians and Ecuadorans, were arrested on suspicion of drug smuggling, Coast Guard spokesman Petty Officer Jeff Hall said.

The Limerick then drifted into Cuban waters, where Cuban coastguard officials boarded and discovered six tonnes of cocaine. "It was a unique incident. I can't recall anything like this ever happening," Hall said.
The captain and crew were flown from Guantanamo to Miami, where they are in detention awaiting trial.

"We now have the cocaine. The Cubans gave it to us. The Colombians are over here and the case is going forward," Fernandez said. The Cuban coastguard officials are ready to testify in the Miami court if needed, he added.
"I don't know if it signals a new era," he said. "Whether it heralds a change of foreign policy is not my business."
Washington last week said there were credible reports drug cartels were using Cuba as a route for smuggling. It put Cuba on its list of "potentially significant" transit countries.

Florida Republican Representative Ileana Ros Lehtinen wrote President Bill Clinton saying involvement in drugs went to the top of the Cuban leadership. "As long as Castro is not seen as a key participant in drug smuggling in our hemisphere, the United States will not reach victory in the war against drugs," Lehtinen, who is of Cuban origin, wrote.
While official links between the two countries are close to nonexistent, the Limerick case follows two other recent law-enforcement contacts.

Prosecutors from Tampa, Florida, flew to Cuba this month to interview relatives of an alleged plane hijacker, and two Miami detectives went to Havana in October in connection with a murder allegedly committed by a Cuban refugee.
U.S. and Cuban officials are also discussing an immigration accord that would end the virtually automatic asylum granted Cubans who flee the communist-ruled island and reach the United States.

Tension between Havana and Washington rose in February, when Cuban jets shot down two planes from a Miami-based exile group, Brothers to the Rescue. Four people were killed and Washington tightened the embargo it imposed on Cuba in 1962.
